entry.title: NB 5 Communications Principles
entry.content:
• Topics
    • Communication Protocols
    • Communication Standards
    • Network Communication Models
A. Introduction
  • Communication requires rules or agreements before it can happen.
  • In networking, these rules are called protocols.

  • Protocols ensure that communication between devices is successful.

  • Objectives
    • Understand communication protocols
    • Understand communication standards
    • Compare OSI and TCP/IP models
B. Communication Protocols
  • Communication happens in different forms and environments.
  • Each situation follows specific rules and expectations.
  • Before communication:
    • The method must be defined
    • The language must be agreed upon
    • Acknowledgement may be required
  • Key Principles
  • Communication requires:
    • Identified sender and receiver
    • Agreed method of communication
    • Common language
    • Proper timing and speed
    • Confirmation or acknowledgement
  1. Why Protocols Matter
    • Computers rely on protocols to communicate.
    • All devices in a network must use the same protocol.
  • Protocol Characteristics
    • Message Format
      • Defines the structure of data being sent
    • Message Size
      • Data may be split into smaller pieces
    • Timing
      • Controls speed and data flow
    • Encoding
      • Converts data into signals (electrical, light, etc.)
    • Encapsulation
      • Adds addressing information to data
    • Message Patterns
      • Some communications require acknowledgements
C. Communication Standards
  1. Devices in a Network
    • Devices only recognize their own addressing information.
    • They rely on protocols to communicate with others.
    • Data is broken into packets for transmission.
    • Examples of Protocol Roles
    • Ethernet / WLAN
      • Connect devices to the network
    • DHCP
      • Assigns IP addresses
    • DNS
      • Translates domain names to IP addresses
    • IP / TCP
      • Ensures delivery of data
  2. The Internet and Standards
    • A standard is a set of rules for how something works.
    • Standards ensure compatibility between devices.
    • Different devices can communicate as long as they follow the same standards.
  3. Standards Organizations
    • Standards are developed and documented through RFCs (Request for Comments).
    • Managed by organizations like:
      • IETF (Internet Engineering Task Force)
D. Network Communication Models
  1. The Protocol Stack
    • Communication uses multiple protocols working together.
    • These protocols are organized into layers.
    • Example Layers
      • Application – User-level communication
      • Transport – Reliable data delivery
      • Internet – Routing data
      • Network Access – Physical transmission
  2. The TCP/IP Model
    • A layered model used for internet communication.
    • Helps visualize how protocols interact.
    • Layers
    • Application
      • Interface for user data
    • Transport
      • Handles communication between devices
    • Internet
      • Determines routing paths
    • Network Access
      • Handles hardware and media
    • Benefits
      • Simplifies design
      • Allows independent changes
      • Provides a common framework
  3. The OSI Model
    • A reference model used to understand networking.
    • Does not define exact protocols, only functions.
    • Purpose
      • Network design
      • Troubleshooting
      • Understanding communication processes
    • OSI Layers
      • 7 – Application
      • 6 – Presentation
      • 5 – Session
      • 4 – Transport
      • 3 – Network
      • 2 – Data Link
      • 1 – Physical
  4. OSI vs TCP/IP
    • Both models describe how networks function.
    • TCP/IP is practical and used in real networks.
    • OSI is conceptual and used for learning.
    • Mapping
      • OSI Layers 5–7 → TCP/IP Application
      • OSI Layer 4 → TCP/IP Transport
      • OSI Layer 3 → TCP/IP Internet
      • OSI Layers 1–2 → TCP/IP Network Access
Layer Description
Application Interface for user data
Transport Handles communication between devices
Internet Determines routing paths
Network Access Handles hardware and media
TCP/IP Model Layers
OSI Layer Description
7 – ApplicationProcess communication
6 – PresentationData representation
5 – SessionManages sessions
4 – TransportReliable delivery
3 – NetworkRouting
2 – Data LinkFrame transfer
1 – PhysicalSignals
 OSI Model Layers
OSI Model TCP/IP Model
Application Application
Presentation
Session
Transport Transport
Network Internet
Data Link Network Access
Physical
OSI Model Mapped to TCP/IP Model
Summary
  • Communication Protocols
    • Rules that allow devices to communicate
    • Include format, timing, encoding, and delivery methods
  • Communication Standards
    • Ensure compatibility between different devices
    • Allow global communication across networks
  • Network Communication Models
    • Organize protocols into layers
    • TCP/IP is used in real-world networking
    • OSI helps in understanding and troubleshooting
entry.summary: overview of communication principles, including protocols, standards, and network models such as OSI and TCP/IP, and how they enable reliable data transmission across networks

entry.title: NB 4 Building a Home Network
entry.content:
• Topics
    • Home Network Basics
    • Wired and Wireless Technologies
    • Wi-Fi Standards
    • Home Router Configuration
A. Introduction
  • A router connects a home network to the internet.
  • Home routers typically have two main ports:
    • Ethernet ports (LAN)
    • Internet ports (WAN)
  • Most home routers also include:
    • A radio antenna
    • A built-in wireless access point
B. Home Network Basics
  1. Tyypical Home Network Setup
    • Most home networks include the following devices:
    • Modem
      • Internet Access: Yes
      • Local Routing: No
      • Wi-Fi: No
      • Notes: Connects the home network to the ISP
    • Router
      • Internet Access: No (needs modem)
      • Local Routing: Yes
      • Wi-Fi: No
      • Notes: Routes data between the modem and the local network
    • Access Point
      • Internet Access: No (needs modem)
      • Local Routing: No
      • Wi-Fi: Yes
      • Notes: Adds wireless capability to a wired network
    • Wireless Router
      • Internet Access: No (needs modem)
      • Local Routing: Yes
      • Wi-Fi: Yes
      • Notes: Combination of a router and an access point
    • Key Points
      • Home networks usually consist of two networks:
      • Public network – Provided by the ISP.
      • Private Ethernet network (LAN) – Used by devices inside the home.
      • A modem converts the signal from the ISP into a format usable by the home network.
      • A wireless router connects devices within the LAN and provides internet access.
  2. Components of a Home Network
    • Devices commonly connected to a home network include:
      • Desktop computers
      • Gaming systems
      • Smart TVs
      • Printers
      • Scanners
      • Security cameras
      • Telephones
      • Smart home devices (e.g., climate control systems)
  3. Typical Home Network Routers
    • Home and small-business routers usually include two main port types:
    • Ethernet (LAN) Ports
      • Connect to the internal switch of the router.
      • Used for wired devices.
      • All devices connected share the same local network.
    • Internet (WAN) Port
      • Connects the router to another network (usually the modem).
      • Provides internet access to the LAN.
    • Additional features:
      • Built-in wireless access point
      • Wireless and wired devices typically share the same LAN by default.
C. Network Technologies in the Home
  1. LAN Wireless Frequencies
    • Most wireless home networks operate on:
      • 2.4 GHz band
      • 5 GHz band
    • Example technologies:
    • Bluetooth
      • Uses 2.4 GHz
      • Short-range, low-speed communication
    • Wi-Fi (IEEE 802.11 standards)
      • Uses 2.4 GHz and 5 GHz bands
  2. Wired Network Technologies
    • Although wireless networking is common, wired connections are still useful for:
      • Faster speeds
      • Lower latency
      • More stable connections
    • Ethernet Protocol
      • Most common wired networking protocol.
      • Uses Ethernet cables to connect devices in a LAN.
    • Common Wired Media
    • Category 5e (Cat5e) Cable
      • Unshielded twisted pair cable
      • Contains 4 twisted wire pairs
      • Used for Ethernet LANs
    • Coaxial Cable
      • Single copper core with shielding
      • Commonly used for:
      • Cable internet
      • Television
      • CCTV systems
    • Fiber-Optic Cable
      • Uses light to transmit data
      • Very high speed and bandwidth
      • Used for long-distance and high-speed internet connections
D. Wireless Standards
  • Wireless devices follow standards to ensure compatibility.
  • The main organization responsible for these standards is the IEEE (Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers).
The Wi-Fi Alliance
Tests wireless devices from different manufacturers to ensure compatibility.
  1. LAN Wireless Frequencies
    • Governed by the IEEE 802.11 standard
    • Different amendments define various Wi-Fi technologies.
    • Uses 2.4 GHz and 5 GHz bands.
  2. Wireless Router Settings
    • Common wireless router settings include:
    • Network Mode
      • Determines supported wireless technologies.
      • Examples: 802.11b, 802.11n, Mixed mode
    • Network Name (SSID)
      • Identifies the wireless network.
      • All devices must use the same SSID to connect.
    • Standard Channel
      • Defines the channel used for wireless communication.
    • SSID Broadcast
      • Controls whether the network name is visible to nearby devices.
    • Important Notes
    • The SSID is:
      • Case-sensitive
      • Up to 32 characters long
      • included in wireless frames to identify the network.
E. Setting Up a Home Router
  • Many home routers include automatic setup utilities for initial configuration.
  1. First-Time Setup
    • To connect a router using a wired connection:
      • Connect an Ethernet patch cable to the computer.
      • Connect the other end to a LAN port on the router.
      • Do not connect to the Internet (WAN) port.
      • Verify the correct internet connection type.
    • Examples:
    • Cable Internet
      • Uses coaxial cable.
    • DSL Internet
      • Uses a telephone cable (RJ-11).
    • Most routers automatically assign an IP address using DHCP.
    • If automatic configuration fails, manually configure:
      • IP address
      • Subnet mask
      • Default gateway
      • DNS server
  2. Network Design Considerations
    • Choosing an SSID
      • Visible to nearby devices if broadcasting is enabled
      • Avoid using: Router brand, Device Model
    • Device Compatibility
      • Some devicees only support older Wi-Fi standards
      • Routers may need legacy mode enabled
      • Legacy mode supports: 802.11a, 802.11b, 802.11g, 802.11n, 802.11ac
      • However, enabling legacy mode may reduce overall network speed.
    • Guest Networks
      • Some routers allow guest SSIDs.
      • Guests can access the internet but not local devices.
F. Packet Tracer Activity

Packet Tracer Activity: Module 4 – Build a Home Network

  • Overview
    • In this Packet Tracer activity, I set up and tested a basic home network environment.
    • The goal was to understand how common home networking devices work together to provide internet connectivity through both wired and wireless connections.
  • What I Did
    • First, I connected the required devices to simulate a typical home network.
      • This included connecting a cable modem, a wireless router, two desktop computers, a laptop, and a television.
    • The modem served as the connection point to the internet service provider

    • The router acted as the central device that allowed the other devices to communicate and access the internet.

    • After establishing the physical connections, I accessed the router’s graphical interface from one of the computers.

    • From there, I configured the necessary settings so the router could manage the network and automatically provide IP addresses to connected devices.

    • I also set up a wireless network so that wireless devices in the home could connect through Wi-Fi.

    • This allowed the laptop to join the network without using an Ethernet cable.

    • Finally, I verified that all devices were able to connect to the network and access an external server.
    • This confirmed that the network was functioning correctly and that both wired and wireless clients could reach the internet.
  • Result
    • At the end of the activity, the simulated home network was successfully configured.
    • All devices were able to obtain network addresses and communicate with external resources, demonstrating how a typical home router manages connectivity for multiple devices.
Summary
  • Home Network Basics
    • Home networks contain both public and private networks.
    • Devices connect to a router to share internet access and communicate locally.
  • Network Technologies
    • Wireless networks use electromagnetic waves.
    • Most home wireless networks operate at 2.4 GHz or 5 GHz.
    • Wired connections (Ethernet) offer stable and fast communication.
  • Wireless Standards
  • Managed by IEEE 802.11.
  • Key router settings include:
    • Network Mode
    • SSID
    • Channel
    • SSID Broadcast
  • Optimizing these settings ensures secure and efficient wireless communication.
entry.summary: explains the fundamentals of home networking components of a typical home network, wired and wireless communication technologies, Wi-Fi standards, and basic router configuration

entry.title: NB 3 Wireless and Mobile Networks
entry.content:
• Topics
    • Wireless Networks
    • Mobile Device Connectivity
A. Wireless Networks
  1. Types of Wireless Networks
    • Phones communicate on many different networks:
      • Voice channel → Cellular provider network
      • Using a Bluetooth device → Bluetooth
      • Communicating over the global internet → Wi-Fi
      • Sending information over extremely short distances (e.g., paying using phones) → Near Field Communication (NFC)
    • Phones are also capable of receiving GPS signals
      • Receiving signals from satellites around the Earth
      • Satellites send signals to devices with GPS capability
  2. Cell Phone Interactions with Different Networks
    • Talk
      • Communicate with landlines, cell phones, and businesses
      • Cell phones contain multiple receivers and transmitters
    • Data
      • Uses a data plan
      • Enables internet access when not near Wi-Fi
      • Uses cellular infrastructure to access the internet
    • Wi-Fi
      • Connects to hotspots and home wireless networks
    • Location Services
      • GPS, maps, and location-based services
    • Pay Services
      • Cash registers, payment pads
      • Uses NFC
  3. Other Wireless Networks
    • Smartphones connect in several ways besides cellular networks

Global Positioning System (GPS)

  • Uses satellites to transmit signals covering the Earth
  • Phones calculate their location within about 10 meters accuracy

Wi-Fi

  • Allows phones to connect to local networks and the internet
  • Requires being within range of a wireless access point

Bluetooth

  • A low-power, short-range wireless technology
  • Replaces wired connections for accessories such as:
    • Speakers
    • Headphones
    • Microphones
    • Smartwatches
  • Can transmit both voice and data
  • Enables multiple devices to communicate simultaneously

Near Field Communication (NFC)

  • Uses electromagnetic fields to transmit data
  • Allows data exchange when devices are very close together (usually a few centimeters)
  • Example: smartphone payment systems
B. Mobile Device Connectivity
  1. Mobile Devices and Wi-Fi
    • Mobile devices allow users to:
      • Work
      • Learn
      • Play
      • Communicate from anywhere
    • Tasks previously requiring large computers can now be completed using mobile devices on wireless networks
    • It is advisable to connect to Wi-Fi instead of cellular data when possible because:
      • Wi-Fi uses less power
      • Helps conserve battery life
    • Security precautions when using Wi-Fi
      • Never send login or password information using plaintext
      • Use a VPN when sending sensitive data
      • Enable security on home networks
      • Use WPA2 or higher encryption
  2. Wi-Fi Settings
    • Two popular mobile operating systems:
      • Android
      • Apple iOS
    • Both provide settings to configure connections to wireless networks
  3. Configure Mobile Wi-Fi Connectivity
    • If a device does not prompt to connect to Wi-Fi:
      • The SSID broadcast may be disabled
      • The device may not be set to connect automatically
    • SSID
      • The name assigned to a wireless network
    • Passphrase
      • The wireless network password
    • SSIDs and passphrases must be typed exactly as configured on the router.
  4. Configure Cellular Data Settings
    • Cellular data plans are provided by mobile carriers
    • Bandwidth and usage costs vary by carrier and plan
    • Mobile devices are typically configured to:
      • Use Wi-Fi first
      • Switch to cellular data when Wi-Fi is unavailable
    • Network transitions are usually automatic:
      • Example: switching from 4G to 3G coverage
      • Connections are typically not interrupted
  5. Simple Connectivity with Bluetooth
    • Devices connect using different methods:
      • Cellular
      • Wi-Fi
      • Wired connections
    • Bluetooth advantages
      • Wireless
      • Automatic
      • Low power consumption
    • Up to eight Bluetooth devices can be connected at the same time.
  6. Bluetooth Pairing
    • Bluetooth pairing occurs when two devices establish a connection to share resources.

Pairing process

  1. Turn on Bluetooth radios
  2. One device searches for other devices
  3. Other devices must be set to discoverable (visible) mode

When discoverable, devices transmit:

  • Device name
  • Bluetooth class
  • Supported services
  • Technical specifications

During pairing:

  • A PIN or passkey may be required
  • The PIN is stored so future connections occur automatically
Summary
  1. Wireless Networks
    • Mobile phones use radio waves to transmit voice signals to cell towers.
    • When a call is made:
      • The signal is relayed between towers until it reaches its destination.
    • Wireless networks are used for:
      • Voice calls
      • Text messages
      • Data transmission
    • The most common cellular network type is GSM.
    • 3G, 4G, 4G-LTE, and 5G
      • Represent enhanced cellular networks optimized for faster data transmission
    • Wi-Fi
      • Allows smartphones to connect to local networks and the internet
      • Often available through public hotspots
    • Bluetooth
      • Enables communication between devices over short distances
    • NFC
      • Allows devices to exchange data at very close range
  2. Mobile Device Connectivity
    • To protect Wi-Fi communications:
      • Never send login credentials in plaintext
      • Use VPNs when sending sensitive data
      • Secure home networks
      • Use WPA2 or stronger encryption
    • Mobile devices:
      • Prefer Wi-Fi when available
      • Use cellular data when Wi-Fi is unavailable
    • Bluetooth technology
      • Enables easy connections between devices and accessories
      • Uses minimal power
    • Bluetooth pairing
    • Requires:
      • Bluetooth enabled
      • Device discovery
      • Discoverable mode
    • A PIN may be required during pairing for authentication.
Questions
  • What are GSM transmitters and receivers?
    • Global System for Mobile Communications (GSM) transmitters and receivers are radio components used in mobile phones and cellular towers to send and receive voice and data signals over cellular networks
    • A transmitter
      • sends radio signals from a mobile device to a nearby cell tower (base station)
    • A receiver
      • receives radio signals from the tower back to the mobile device
    • In a GSM network,
      1. A phone transmits a signal (a voice, text, or data) to the nearest cell tower
      2. The tower receives the signal and forwards it throught the carrier’s network
      3. The signal is routed to another tower near the destination.
      4. That tower trransmits the signal to the receiving phone.
    • These transmitters and receivers allow phones to communicate wirelessly using radio frequencies instead of physical cables


  • What is the difference between 3G, 4G, 5G, and Wi-Fi?
    • the main difference is how the network is provided and how devices connect to it.
Technology Type Main Use Key Feature
3G Cellular network Mobile internet and calls Early mobile data
4G/4G-LTE Cellular network Faster mobile internet supports streaming, video calls, and apps
5G Cellular network Very high-speed mobile internet Lower latency and much faster speeds
Wi-Fi Local wireless network Internet access in homes,, offices, and hotspots Uses a router instead of cellular towers


  • Is the statement “Up to eight Bluetooth devices can be connected together at any one time” still accurate?
    • Yes, but it depends on the Bluetooth setup
    • Classic Bluetooth (piconet)
      • one master device
      • up to 7 connected devices
      • common for headphones, speakers, keyboards, mice
    • Bluetoot Low Energy (BLE)
      • can support many more devices, depending on the hardware and software implementation
      • used in modern devices like smartwatces, IoT devices, and sensors
Reflection

Wireless and mobile networks allow devices to send and receive data without physical cables, enabling communication, internet access, and device interaction through wireless technologies.
entry.summary: explores how mobile devices communicate using different wireless technologies

entry.title: NB 2 Network Components, Types, and Connections

link.title: NB 2 Network Components, Types, and Connections

entry.content:
• Topics
    • Network Types
    • Network Components
    • Network Connections
    • Client and Server Roles
    • ISP Connectivity Options
A. Clients and Servers
  • Computer hosts can act as:
    • Client
    • Server
    • Both
  • The role of a device depends on the software installed.
  • Servers
    • Provide information or services to other hosts
    • Examples: email servers, web servers
  • Clients
    • Request and display information from servers
    • Example: web browsers like Chrome
  • Example interactions
    • Client requests a webpage from a web server
    • Web server responds with the webpage
    • Email clients (Outlook) access email from email servers
    • Clients can send and receive emails through the server
  • Service Types
    • Email
      • Runs email server software
      • Clients use mail client software like Outlook
    • Web
      • Runs web server software
      • Clients access through browsers like Chrome
    • File
      • Runs file server software
      • Stores files in a central location
      • Accessed through tools like Windows File Explorer
  1. Client and Server Roles
    • Hosts
      • Computers connected to a network
      • Participate directly in communication
      • Can send and receive messages
    • Servers
      • Provide services to other hosts
      • Each service requires separate server software
      • Websites visited online are hosted on servers connected to the internet
    • Clients
      • Request information from servers
      • Examples: Chrome, Safari
  2. Peer-to-Peer Networks
    • Client and server software usually run on separate computers
    • However, one computer can run both
    • In small businesses or homes:
      • Devices can act as both servers and clients
    • Simplest P2P network
      • Two directly connected computers
      • Wired or wireless connection
      • Devices exchange data and services
    • Advantages
      • Easy to set up
      • Less complex
      • Lower cost
      • Useful for file sharing and printer sharing
    • Disadvantages
      • No centralized administration
      • Less secure
      • Not scalable
      • Performance can slow when devices act as both client and server
  3. Peer-to-Peer Applications
    • A P2P application allows a device to act as:
      • Client
      • Server
    • Every client can also be a server
    • Devices can:
      • Send messages
      • Receive messages simultaneously
    • Hybrid P2P systems
      • Resource sharing is decentralized
      • Indexes are stored in a centralized directory
      • Peers query the index server to locate resources
  4. Multiple Roles in a Network
    • A computer with server software can serve multiple clients simultaneously
    • One computer can run multiple server software
    • One computer can also run multiple client software
    • A host can connect to multiple servers at the same time
      • Example: checking email, browsing the web, instant messaging, streaming internet radio
B. Network Components
  1. Network Infrastructure
    • Network paths can range from:
      • A single cable between two computers
      • A global network spanning the world
    • Network infrastructure
      • The platform supporting network communication
      • Provides stable communication channels
    • Three hardware categories
      • End devices
      • Intermediary devices
      • Network media
    • Hardware examples
      • Laptop
      • Switch
      • Router
      • Access point
      • Network cables
    • Some components are invisible
      • Wireless media using radio frequencies or infrared
  2. End Devices
    • Also called hosts
    • Interface between users and the network
    • Examples
      • Computers
      • Printers
      • Telephones
      • CCTV cameras
      • Mobile devices
    • Can be:
      • Message source
      • Message destination
    • Hosts are identified using addresses
    • When communication starts
      • The sender uses the destination address
C. ISP Connectivity Options
  1. ISP Services
    • Internet Service Provider (ISP)
      • Connects home networks to the internet
    • Examples of ISPs
      • Cable providers
      • Telephone service providers
      • Cellular networks
      • Independent providers leasing bandwidth
    • Additional services
      • Email accounts
      • Website hosting
      • Network storage
      • Backup and security services
    • ISPs connect with other ISPs
      • Forming the global internet
    • Internet backbone
      • High-speed fiber-optic infrastructure
      • Connects service provider networks worldwide
  2. ISP Connections
    • Internet backbone consists of
      • Fiber-optic cables
      • High-performance routers and switches
    • Simple connection
      • Computer → Modem → ISP
      • Less secure
    • Common connection
      • Computer → Router → ISP
      • Router provides:
    • Security
    • IP addressing
    • Wired and wireless connectivity
  3. Cable and DSL Connections
    • Most home users connect through:
      • Cable
      • DSL (Digital Subscriber Line)
    • Cable
      • Uses coaxial cable from cable TV providers
      • High bandwidth
      • Always-on connection
    • DSL
      • Uses telephone lines
      • Splits the line into channels:
    • Voice calls
    • Download data
    • Upload data * Speed depends on - Line quality - Distance from the provider’s central office
  4. Additional Connectivity Options
    • Cellular
      • Uses mobile networks
      • Available where cellular signal exists
      • Often metered
    • Satellite
      • Useful where cable/DSL is unavailable
      • Requires clear line of sight
      • Higher installation costs
    • Dial-up
      • Uses telephone line and modem
      • Low bandwidth
      • Mostly obsolete
    • Fiber connections
      • Increasingly common in cities
      • Provide very high bandwidth
Summary
  1. Clients and Servers
    • All computers connected to a network are hosts
    • Hosts can act as:
      • Clients
      • Servers
      • Both
    • P2P networks
      • Easy to set up
      • Low cost
      • Suitable for small networks
    • Limitations
      • Less security
      • No central management
      • Limited scalability
  2. Network Components
    • Network infrastructure supports communication
    • Three hardware categories
      • End devices
      • Intermediate devices
      • Network media
    • Examples of end devices
      • Computers
      • Printers
      • Phones
      • CCTV
      • Mobile devices
  3. ISP Connectivity
    • ISPs connect home networks to the internet
    • ISPs interconnect to form the global internet
    • Common home connections
      • Cable
      • DSL
    • Other options
      • Cellular
      • Satellite
      • Dial-up
Reflection
  • A network is like assembling furniture
  • The parts represent network components
  • The finished structure represents the complete network
  • Proper assembly ensures a functional and organized system
entry.summary: overview of network types, components, connections, and client-server roles.

entry.title: NB 1 Communications in a Connected World

link.title: NB 1 Communications in a Connected World

entry.content:
• Topics
    • Network Types
    • Data Transmission
    • Bandwidth and Throughput
A. Network Types
  • Everything is Online
    • Devices today are expected to always be connected to the global internet.
    • The internet is used to interact and communicate with others.
    • The internet is not a physical place but a collection of connections.
    • It is a platform to find and share information.
  • Who owns the Internet?
    • No single entity owns the internet.
    • It is a worldwide collection of interconnected networks.
    • Networks cooperate to exchange information using common standards (protocols).
    • Connections use:
      • Telephone wires
      • Fiber-optic cables
      • Wireless transmissions
      • Satellite links
    • All online resources exist somewhere within the global internet.
    • These destinations connect to local networks that send and receive data.
  1. Mobile Devices
    • The internet connects devices used daily, such as:
    • Mobile phones
    • Smartwatches
    • Smart glasses
    • Other smart home devices
  2. Connected Home Devices
    • Many home devices can connect to the internet for remote monitoring, including:
    • Security systems
    • Appliances
    • Smart TVs
    • Gaming consoles
  3. Other Connected Devices
    • Devices outside the home also connect to networks, including:
    • Examples
    • Smart cars
    • RFID tags
    • Sensors and actuators
    • Medical devices * Sensors and Actuators
    • Sensors detect environmental conditions:
      • Temperature
      • Humidity
      • Pressure
      • Soil moisture
    • Actuators perform actions based on sensor data:
      • Example: triggering irrigation when soil is dry
  4. Local Networks
    • Networks come in many sizes.
    • They can range from two computers to hundreds of thousands of devices.
  • Small Home Networks
    • Connect a few devices together such as:
      • Computers
      • Printers
      • Internet connection
  • Small Office/Home Office (SOHO) Networks
    • Used in small offices or homes.
    • Allow sharing of resources such as:
      • Printers
      • Documents
      • Pictures
      • Music
    • Networks provide faster and cheaper communication than traditional methods.
    • Enable rapid communication such as:
      • Email
      • Instant messaging
    • Provide centralized access to information stored on servers.
    • Allow home or remote office computers to connect to a corporate network.
    • Enable access to centralized shared resources.
  • Medium to Large Networks
    • Used by organizations such as:
      • Corporations
      • Schools
    • May connect hundreds or thousands of hosts across multiple locations.
  • Worldwide Networks
    • The internet itself.
    • A network of networks connecting millions of computers worldwide.
B. Data Transmission
  • What is Data?
    • Data is raw information that users send, share, or upload.
  1. Types of (Personal) Data
    • Volunteered Data
      • Data willingly shared by individuals.
    • Inferred Data
      • Data generated from user activities.
      • Often collected without the user realizing.
      • Example: Credit card transactions showing preferences or locations.
    • Observed Data
      • Data collected and stored automatically.
      • Example:
    • Location data from mobile applications.
  2. The Bit
    • Computers operate using binary digits (bits):
      • 0 or 1
    • A bit can represent:
      • Two voltage levels
      • On or off states
      • Input devices convert human actions into binary.
      • Output devices convert binary into human-readable information.
ASCII (American Standard Code for Information Interchange)
A common binary encoding system.

Examples:

  • A = 0100 0001
  • 9 = 0011 1001

  • (#) = 0010 0011

  • 8 bits = 1 byte
C. Methods of Data Transmission
  • After data becomes binary, it must be converted into signals.
  • Transmission Media
    • Signals travel through different media such as:
      • Copper wires
      • Fiber-optic cables
      • Wireless electromagnetic waves
    • Signals may travel as:
      • Electrical pulses
      • Light pulses
      • Radio waves
  • Signals may be converted multiple times before reaching the destination.
  1. Three Common Signal Transmission Methods
  • Electrical Signals
    • Data transmitted as electrical pulses through copper wires.
  • Optical Signals
    • Electrical signals converted into light pulses using fiber-optic cables.
  • Wireless Signals
    • Data transmitted using:
      • Infrared
      • Microwave
      • Radio waves
  • Most homes and small businesses use:
    • Copper cables
    • Wi-Fi wireless connections
  • Large networks often use fiber-optic cables for longer distances.
D. Bandwidth and Throughput
  • Different media support data transfer at different speeds.
  • Two key measurements:
    • Throughput
    • Bandwidth
  1. Throughput
    • Throughput measures the actual amount of data successfully transferred over time.
    • Throughput is usually lower than bandwidth because of factors such as:
    • Network traffic
    • Type of data transmitted
    • Network device delays
  2. Bandwidth

  • Bandwidth refers to the capacity of a network medium to carry data

  • Digital Bandwidth
    • Measures the amount of data that can travel between two points over time
    • Common Units:
      • Kbps – thousands of bits per second
      • Mbps – millions of bits per second
      • Gbps – billions of bits per second
  • Factors Affecting Bandwidth
    • Physical properties of the medium
    • Current technology
    • Laws of physics

  • Latency
    • Latency is the time delay for data to travel from source to destination.
  • Network Limitation
    • In a network path:
      • Throughput cannot exceed the slowest link in the network.
E. Internet Speed Tests
  • Tools used to measure network performance include:
    • Speedtest.net
  • Measurements include:
    • Download speed – bits received per second
    • Upload speed – bits sent per second
  • These tools measure performance across:
    • Local networks
    • Internet service providers
    • Internet connections
Summary
  • Network Types
    • The internet is a global network of interconnected networks.
    • Networks exchange data using standard protocols.
    • Connections may use:
      • Wired cables
      • Fiber-optic cables
      • Wireless transmission
      • Satellite links
    • SOHO networks connect home or small office devices.
    • Large networks connect organizations across multiple locations.

  • Data Transmission
    • Types of Personal Data
      • Volunteered data – intentionally shared
      • Observed data – collected by monitoring actions
      • Inferred data – derived from analyzing other data

  • Bit
    • Smallest unit of data
    • Represented as 0 or 1

  • Transmission Methods
    • Electrical signals
    • Optical signals
    • Wireless signals

  • Bandwidth and Throughput
    • Bandwidth
      • Maximum data capacity of a medium
      • Measured in:
        • Kbps
        • Mbps
        • Gbps
    • Throughput
      • Actual data transferred
      • Influenced by:
        • Network traffic
        • Latency
        • Network device delays

  • Latency
    • Time delay for data to travel between two points.
Reflection
  • The internet is a massive network of networks connected directly or indirectly.
  • It can be visualized like a spider’s web, where many connections link the systems together.
entry.summary: overview of network communication concepts, including network types, data transmission, and the fundamentals of bandwidth and throughput.

entry.title: Linux File System and Commands
entry.content:
The Linux File System

An overview of the Linux File System

  • The Linux File System
    • the directory structure Linux uses to store, organize, and access files
    • Everything in Linux is treated as a file, such as
      • programs, logs, devices, configs, network interfaces

Key Linux Directories

Directory What is Inside Purpose Why it Matters What to Look For
/ All system directories the root of the file system It’s the starting point  
/home User home folders, user files for storing non-root user data Look for SSH keys, configs, flags .ssh/id_rsa, .bash_history
/root Root user’s home directory for admin (root) account files If you have access, you gain control of the full system flags, sensitive configurations
/etc Configuration files for system-wide configurations users, passwords, sudo rules passwd, shadow, sudoers
/bin Essential system commands for core binaries needed by all users users, passwords, sudo rules SUID binaries for privilege escalation
/sbin System admin binaries for Admin-level system tools Often abused if misconfigured admin binaries
/usr/bin User programs and utilities for installed user-level binaries Abusable binaries, PATH hijacking abusable binaries
/usr/sbin Admin tools (non-essential) for advanced system management Possible SUID or weak permissions system tools
/var Logs, caches, spool files for variable run time data Log anaalysis, log poisoning, credentials logs
/var/log Systems and application logs for storing logs Auth logs, web logs, forensic clues auth.log, access.log
/tmp Temporary files for short-lived, world-writable storage Upload payloads, execute scripts uploaded payloads
/dev Device files Interface for the hardware Used in reverse shells and I/O redirection /dev/tcp, /dev/tty for reverse shells
/proc Process and system information Virtual file system Leak environment variables, running processes env varriables, process info
/opt Optional/third-party software External applications Often poorly secured custom apps custom apps, scripts
/lib Shared libraries Libraries required by binaries Library hijacking attacks  
/mnt Mountd file systems for temporary mount points Access external or mounted drives mounted drives
/media Removable media USBs, CDs, external devices Data leakage opportunities removable storage
/srv Service data for data served by services Web or FTP content  
/var/www Web server files Website content Web shells, source code leaks website source code, configuration files
/boot Bootloader files for System boot data Rare target; kernel attacks kernel files
/run Runtime process data for storing temporary system information Rare target; kernel attacks sockets and sessions
/lost+found Recovered files for file system recovery For looking at discarded or recovered files  


Linux Commands

An overview of some Linux commands organized by use


General Commands

An overview of some generic Linux commands

Navigation Commands

Command What it Does Purpose Example
pwd Shows current directory For orientation to see where I am  
cd Changes directory Moving around the filesystem cd [directory]
cd .. → go up one level
cd ~ → go to home directory
cd / → go to root
man Shows command manuals For providing command documentations for options and usage explanations  
ls Shows detailed listing of the directories For checking permissions ls -la
tree Shows the directory structure For visual recon  


Searching & Filtering Commands

Command What it Does Purpose Example
grep Search text For finding credentials grep "root" /etc/passwd
grep -R "password" /etc → recursive search
find Finding files For looking and hunting for loots find / -name "*.conf"
locate Finding files using a databse For searching files quickly locate [filename]


File Creating, Viewing, Editing, and Management Commands

Command What it Does Purpose Example
cp Copy contents of files For quick duplicates cp [source file] [destination file]
mv Moves files/ renames files For renaming/moving files mv [old_name] [new_name]
rm Deletes files or directories For deleting to cause unavailability rm [old_name] or rm -r [directory name]
mkdir Creates directory For creating directories mkdir [directory name]
rmdir Deletes empty directories For deleting empty directories rmdir [directory name]
nano Terminal text editor For editing writable files nano [filename]
vi/wim Advanced text editor For editing writable files, common on servers vim [filename]
touch Creates empty files For creating new files instantly, also updates file timestamps touch [filename]
echo Write text to a file For scripting echo "hi" > [filename] → writing text to a file
echo "hi" >> [filename] → appending text to a file (persistent)
cat Prints entire file For viewing small files cat [filename]
less Displays a scrollable viewer of a file For viewing large files less [filename]
head Displays the first 10 lines of a file For a quick preview head [filename]
tail Displays the last lines of a file and live logs For monitoring logs tail -f [filename]


File Transfers, Downloads, and Payloads Commands

Command What it Does Purpose Example
wget Downloads files For downloading files and even payloads wget [url]
curl Fetches data For reverse shells curl [url]


Networking & Services Commands

Command What it Does Purpose Example
ip a Shows network interfaces For looking at the whole network  
ss For showing listening services For looking at local ports ss -tulpn or netsat -tulpn (older version)
arp For showing neighboring networks For lateral movement arp -a


Penetration Testing Commands

An overview of the most commonly used commands in penetration testing engagements


System & User Enumeration Commands

Command What it Does Purpose Example
whoami Shows current user For checking privilege level  
hostname Shows system name For target identification  
id Shows User ID, groups For sudo/group abuse  
uname Shows kernel information For checking Kernel exploits uname -a
lsb_release Shows OS version To match exploits to use lsb_release -a
uptime Shows system runtime For checking stability  
ps Displays running processes For showing active processes to monitor system activity  
du Shows directory sizes For finding large data du -sh *


User & Home Directory Recon

Command What it Does Purpose Example
ls /home Shows users For finding targets  
ls -la ~ Shows hidden files For looking for SSH keys, history  
cat ~/.bash_history Shows command history For looking for credentials, tools  
find /home -name "*.txt" For finding files For looking for flags and notes  


Looking for Credentials Commands

Command What it Does Purpose Example
cat /etc/passwd Shows users For finding valid accounts  
cat /etc/shadow Shows password hashes For offline tracking  
env Shows environment variables For looking for API keys, tokens  


Permissions & Ownerships Commands

Command What it Does Purpose Example
chmod Changes permissions For executing payloads chmod +x script.sh
chown Changes owner For persisting attacks chown root:root file
ls -l Views permissions For finding weak files
entry.summary: a list of Linux commands and an overview of the Linux File System

entry.title: CTFs - Pickle Rick
entry.content:
The other CTFs are here on this page! 🐳

  • This Rick and Morty TryHackMe challenge requires me to:
    • exploit a web server;
    • and find three ingredients to
      • help Rick make his potion;
      • and transform himself back into a human from a pickle
  • I first deployed the virtual machine and explore the web application

Before going in to the exploration part, I first thought about the phases of Penetration Testing as a guide on what to do first.

The phases of Penetration Testing is as follows:

Reconnaissance → Scanning → Vulnerability Analysis → Exploitation → Post-Exploitation → Reporting

  • Reconnaissance
    • learning anything as much as possible about the target
    • examples: DNS records, WHOIS, Public IPs, OSINT, ping sweeps, port scanning)
  • Scanning and Enumeration
    • identifying vulnerabilities
    • examples: port scanning, service and version detection, OS detection, user enumeration
    • tools that can be used: nmap
  • Vulnerability Analysis
    • identifying weaknesses that can be exploited with the discovered vulnerabilities
    • examples: using known CVEs, misconfigurations, weak credentials, outdated software, logic flaws
    • tools that can be used: Nessus, OpenVas, Nikto
  • Exploitation
    • gaining unauthorized access
    • examples: password attacks, web exploits
    • tools that can be used: Metasploit
  • Post-Exploitation
    • seeing how far this attack can go by:
      • escalating privileges, moving laterally, credential dumping, accessing sensitive data
    • example: escalating from a low-privilege user to root/admin
  • Reporting
    • reporting findings of vulnerabilities found, risk levels, impact, and even recommendations

Scanning

  • With that, I first started scanning the machine for any open ports

I saw that the SSH port and HTTP port is open so I might explore these two further.

Vulnerability Analysis

An open SSH port (port 22) is an opportunity for later if I have credentials. On the other hand, an open HTTP port (port 80) can be a good starting place as I can do a lot in that area.

Typing in the IP address in a Firefox browser showed me this web page.

Trying to view its page source code showed me this:

It doesnt really show anything except for a username. I’ll take note of this for later

The next thing I can do now that I have a web page is to look for directories I can access using a tool called dirb.

Exploitation

I found out that I can access these webpages. Let’s see what I can find from these.

I found this on the robots.txt path from earlier. A quick google search told me that a robots.txt file tells search engine crawlers to not go there, as per the Robots Exclusion Protocol.

With that, developers accidentally use it as hide stuff list that reads to pentesters as “please attack these first”. It’s basically a page where developers don’t want people to look at. So, it must be important hehe let’s take note of this for later.

It wasnt much so maybe I might be missing something. I tried to look at the documentation of dirb and figured out a more specific command I can try.

One example I can try is to append the -X command to also look for webpages that have different extensions.

A quick google search later for the different extensions for webpages show the following: php, html, js, txt, bak, old, zip, env. So, I will use these first.

The command dirb [target site] -X .php showed that I can access these webpages.

Going to the login.php page directly showed me this login page.

If I remember clearly, when I checked the source code of the page, there showed a username. I can also try to use the random word I saw earlier in the /robots.txt page.

And I got in!

It says command panel so maybe I can try some commands. I typed in dir -a and it showed the following:

These are all web pages from the website. Maybe i can access them by appending the file names to the path of the website, starting from the most suspicious file name: http://10.48.176.26/Sup3rS3cretPickl3Ingred.txt

And it showed this: the first ingredient!

For finding out the next ingredient, I accessed the /clue.txt page and it showed this:

Post-Exploitation

Now, the Linux File System is how Linux organizes, stores, and accesses files and directories.

  • / → everything
  • /etc → configs
  • /home → users
  • /var → logs & web data
  • /tmp → temporary stuff
  • /bin → commands
  • /root → admin home

I can start by going through those directories

Trying dir / -a showed the directories of the filesystem

Trying dir /home -a showed rick’s account. Let’s try to snoop there.

Trying dir /home/rick -a showed this:

I tried the command cat /home/rick/second\ ingredients to display its contents and it showed me this:

Since this is clearly a file, I can try to use less and more to view it. The command more didn’t work, but less did.

I tried the command less /home/rick/second\ ingredients to display its contents and it showed me this:

I got the 2nd ingredient!

Next, I tried if I can use sudo -l so I can escalate my own privileges. And I can!

So, I tried sudo dir /root -a and it showed me this:

I tried to use the command sudo less /root/3rd.text to try to display its contents as I think that is the 3rd ingredient and it showed me the 3rd ingredient!

After inputting these answers in the answer fields, I finished the Pickle Rick CTF and turned Rick back into a human!
entry.summary: a Rick and Morty CTF, Rick needs help turning back into a human

entry.title: Capture the Flag (CTF) Challenges
entry.content:
I plan to actively work through and complete the CTF challenges mentioned in this guide as part of my hands-on cybersecurity learning journey! 🐳

🕵🏻‍♀️ Beginner Friendly CTF Challenges in TryHackMe

CTFs simulate real-world cyberattacks in controlled environments. Many challenges are inspired by actual breaches, letting beginners experience how attacks happen without any legal or ethical risk.

Top Beginner CTF Challenges (2025)

These challenges are widely considered approachable—even for complete beginners:

  • Pickle Rick – Web enumeration and command injection basics
  • Basic Pentesting – Network scanning and SSH brute-force concepts
  • RootMe – File upload bypass and privilege escalation
  • Simple CTF – Reconnaissance and credential discovery
  • Bounty Hacker – Sudo misconfigurations and privilege abuse
  • LazyAdmin – Directory discovery and CMS exploitation

Core Skills

Beginner-friendly CTFs help develop the exact skills employers look for:

  • Network Scanning & Enumeration – using tools like Nmap
  • Web Application Testing – aligned with OWASP principles
  • Linux Command Line Skills – file navigation, permissions, and privilege escalation
  • Analytical Thinking – solving problems methodically under pressure

Tips for CTF Success

  • Start Small – Build confidence with easier challenges first
  • Take Notes – Record commands, mistakes, and lessons learned
  • Join Communities – TryHackMe Discord, Reddit, and cybersecurity forums
  • Be Consistent – One challenge per week beats irregular cramming
  • Use Hints Strategically – Walkthroughs aren’t cheating if used to understand gaps, research concepts, and retry challenges independently

What Comes After Beginner CTFs?

After completing your first few challenges, you can progress to:

  • Competitive CTFs and cyber leagues
  • Advanced labs and real-world simulations
  • Certification paths such as SAL1 and PT1
  • Entry-level roles in penetration testing or security analysis

Final Thoughts

Every cybersecurity professional starts somewhere—and for most, that place is CTFs. The skills you gain through beginner challenges directly translate to real-world defense and offensive security work. With steady practice, you’re building the same foundation used by professionals today.
entry.summary: a guide to some beginner-friendly CTF Challenges
